nodeData.note: Edexcel International GCSE English Language A, Paper 1, code 4EA1 slash 01. Two hours fifteen minutes, 90 marks, 60 percent of the grade. Section A is reading, 45 marks, about an hour and a half. Section B is writing, 45 marks, about 45 minutes. Each branch is one question type: read the question, find the key words, plan, write, check. Then five spoken questions. Draft for teacher review. (Source: spec page 5.)

children.note: Question 1 is worth 2 marks and tests reading, which is assessment objective 1. You choose two words or phrases from a few given lines of the unseen text. Spend about two or three minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 12; spec page 29.)
Listen for the line numbers and for who or what you must describe. That is all the question asks. (Source: SAMs PDF page 12.)
Underline the line numbers and the person or thing named. In 2025 some students described the wrong person. (Source: June 2025 report page 5.)
No plan needed. Put a finger on the first line and the last line you are allowed to use. (Source: SAMs PDF page 12.)
Copy two short words or phrases exactly from those lines. Write one on each answer line. Do not explain them. (Source: June 2025 report page 5.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Picking words from outside the given lines. June 2025 report page 5, and June 2023 report page 5.
Describing the wrong person or thing. June 2025 report page 5.
Using your own words or adding an explanation, which gets no marks. June 2025 report page 5.
Copying out all the lines instead of choosing. June 2025 report page 5.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many marks is Question 1? Answer: Two marks, one for each word or phrase. (Source: SAMs PDF page 12; spec page 29.)
Ask: Where must your words come from? Answer: Only from the lines the question gives you. (Source: SAMs PDF page 12; spec page 29.)
Ask: Do you use your own words? Answer: No. You copy words or phrases from the text. (Source: SAMs PDF page 12; spec page 29.)
Ask: Should you explain your choice? Answer: No. An explanation earns nothing here. (Source: SAMs PDF page 12; spec page 29.)
Ask: How long should it take? Answer: About two or three minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 12; spec page 29.)

Question 2 is worth 4 marks and tests reading, assessment objective 1. You describe or explain something from given lines of the unseen text, in your own words. Spend about five minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 13; spec page 29.)
Listen for three things: the lines, the topic, and the words in your own words. (Source: SAMs PDF page 13.)
Mark the line numbers, the topic, and the word describe or explain. (Source: June 2025 report page 10.)
Find four different points in those lines. Number them one to four. One extra point is a safe idea. (Source: June 2025 report page 10.)
Write each point as a short sentence in your own words. Do not copy the text and do not give your opinion. (Source: June 2023 report page 9.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Fewer than four points, or the same point twice. June 2025 report page 10.
Copying the text instead of using your own words. June 2025 report page 10, and June 2023 report page 9.
Going outside the given lines, or giving a general overview. June 2025 report page 10.
Listing points too briefly when the question says describe. June 2025 report page 10.
Giving your own opinion instead of points. June 2023 report page 9.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many marks is Question 2? Answer: Four marks. (Source: SAMs PDF page 13; spec page 29.)
Ask: What does in your own words mean? Answer: Say it yourself; do not copy whole phrases from the text. (Source: SAMs PDF page 13; spec page 29.)
Ask: How many points should you make? Answer: At least four different points, and one extra is safe. (Source: SAMs PDF page 13; spec page 29.)
Ask: Is your opinion rewarded here? Answer: No. Only points from the given lines. (Source: SAMs PDF page 13; spec page 29.)
Ask: How long should it take? Answer: About five minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 13; spec page 29.)

Question 3 is worth 5 marks and tests reading, assessment objective 1. You explain what we learn from given lines of the unseen text. You may use short quotations to support your points. Spend about seven minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 14; spec page 29.)
Listen for the lines and the topic. Hear the words may support with brief quotations. (Source: SAMs PDF page 14.)
Mark the line numbers, the topic, and the word explain. (Source: June 2025 report page 14.)
Work through the lines from top to bottom. Find five different points. (Source: June 2025 report page 14.)
Make five clear points. Each point is your explanation, with a short quotation only if it helps. (Source: June 2025 report page 83.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Fewer than five points, or the same point twice. June 2025 report page 14.
Quoting without explaining. June 2025 report page 14, and June 2023 report page 14.
Long quotations cut with dots instead of one exact point. June 2023 report page 14.
Analysing language here, which is not needed. June 2023 report page 66.
Writing far too much for five marks. June 2025 report page 14.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many points for Question 3? Answer: Five clear points. (Source: SAMs PDF page 14; spec page 29.)
Ask: Is a quotation alone enough? Answer: No. You must explain the point; the quote only supports it. (Source: SAMs PDF page 14; spec page 29.)
Ask: Should you analyse language here? Answer: No. That is Question 4. (Source: SAMs PDF page 14; spec page 29.)
Ask: Where do your points come from? Answer: Only the lines the question gives. (Source: SAMs PDF page 14; spec page 29.)
Ask: How long should it take? Answer: About seven minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 14; spec page 29.)

Question 4 is worth 12 marks and tests analysis, assessment objective 2. It is on the Anthology text. You explain how the writer uses language and structure to achieve an effect. Spend about twenty minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 15; spec page 29.)
Listen for the effect the question names. Every point must link back to that effect. (Source: SAMs PDF page 15.)
Mark the word how, the word language, the word structure, and the named effect. (Source: June 2025 report page 20.)
Choose four or five moments from the beginning, middle and end. Mark at least one about structure. (Source: June 2025 report page 20.)
For each: name the device, give a short quotation, then say what effect it has on the reader. Start straight away, with no general introduction. (Source: SAMs mark scheme PDF page 42.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Naming features without saying their effect. June 2025 report page 20, and June 2023 report page 19.
Retelling the story, or drifting off the question. June 2025 report page 20.
Writing only about the start of the extract. June 2025 report page 20.
Showing you understand the ideas, but not how language and structure carry them. June 2025 report page 20.
Bullet points and general introductions, which earn nothing. June 2023 report pages 19 and 66.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Which text is Question 4 on? Answer: The Anthology text. (Source: SAMs PDF page 15; spec page 29.)
Ask: What is the key word in the question? Answer: How. Focus on how the writer does it. (Source: SAMs PDF page 15; spec page 29.)
Ask: Do you need both language and structure? Answer: Yes. Both, though not equally. (Source: SAMs PDF page 15; spec page 29.)
Ask: What follows each quotation? Answer: Its effect on the reader. (Source: SAMs PDF page 15; spec page 29.)
Ask: How long should it take? Answer: About twenty minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 15; spec page 29.)

Question 5 is worth 22 marks and tests comparison, assessment objective 3. You compare how the two writers present their ideas and perspectives, with examples from both texts. It is almost half the reading marks. Spend about forty minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 18; spec page 29.)
Listen for compare, both writers, and ideas and perspectives. (Source: SAMs PDF page 18.)
Mark compare, both texts, and the topic the question names. (Source: June 2025 report page 34.)
Draw a quick two-circle diagram. Write what is the same and what is different: ideas, tone, purpose, voice, language. (Source: June 2025 report page 34.)
Each paragraph compares both texts at once, with a short quotation from each and what the difference shows. (Source: June 2025 report page 83.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Only obvious, factual links between the texts. June 2025 report page 35, and June 2023 report page 33.
Retelling each text instead of comparing them. June 2023 report page 33.
Points without evidence from the texts. June 2025 report page 35.
Naming techniques without explaining their effect. June 2023 report page 33.
Not leaving enough time for this question. June 2023 report page 33.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many marks is Question 5? Answer: Twenty-two, almost half of the reading marks. (Source: SAMs PDF page 18; spec page 29.)
Ask: What must every paragraph do? Answer: Talk about both texts together. (Source: SAMs PDF page 18; spec page 29.)
Ask: Name three things you can compare. Answer: For example ideas, tone, purpose, voice or language. (Source: SAMs PDF page 18; spec page 29.)
Ask: What does each point need? Answer: Evidence from the texts. (Source: SAMs PDF page 18; spec page 29.)
Ask: How long should it take? Answer: About forty minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 18; spec page 29.)

Section B gives you a choice of two writing tasks, Question 6 or Question 7. It is worth 45 marks: 27 for communication and 18 for accuracy, assessment objectives 4 and 5. The form may be an article, speech, letter, guide, review, or leaflet. Spend about forty-five minutes. (Source: spec pages 9, 11 and 29.)
Listen for four things: the form, the audience, the purpose, and the topic. (Source: SAMs PDF page 24.)
Mark the form, who you are writing for, and why. Choose the task you have most ideas for. (Source: spec page 9.)
Spend five to eight minutes. Pick two or three ideas you can develop, and plan a strong ending. (Source: June 2023 report page 49.)
Use the right layout and voice for the form. Develop each idea in full paragraphs. Vary your sentences and keep the tone right for the audience. (Source: SAMs writing grids PDF pages 48 to 49.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Unsure of the form or audience, for example a guide that reads like an article. June 2025 report page 68, and June 2023 report page 61.
Bare bullet lists that show no range of sentences. June 2025 report page 68.
Ideas not developed, or an ending that fizzles out. June 2025 report page 51, and June 2023 report page 61.
Missing punctuation, and no time left to check. June 2025 report page 51.
Invented statistics, or handwriting that cannot be read. June 2025 report page 68, and June 2023 report page 61.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many marks is Section B? Answer: Forty-five: 27 for communicating, 18 for accuracy. (Source: spec pages 9, 11 and 29.)
Ask: Name the four things to find in the task. Answer: Form, audience, purpose and topic. (Source: spec pages 9, 11 and 29.)
Ask: Name three forms that may be set. Answer: For example article, speech, letter, guide, review or leaflet. (Source: spec pages 9, 11 and 29.)
Ask: Are bullet lists a good idea? Answer: Not on their own; develop ideas in full sentences. (Source: spec pages 9, 11 and 29.)
Ask: What do you save five minutes for? Answer: Checking spelling and punctuation. (Source: spec pages 9, 11 and 29.)

nodeData.note: Edexcel International GCSE English Language A, Paper 2, code 4EA1 slash 02: Poetry and Prose Texts and Imaginative Writing. One hour thirty minutes, 60 marks, 40 percent of the grade. Section A is one 30-mark essay on a poem or prose text from Part 2 of the Anthology, about 45 minutes. Section B is one 30-mark imaginative writing task from a choice of three, about 45 minutes. How it differs from Paper 1: Paper 1 is two hours fifteen, 90 marks, on non-fiction. Paper 2 has one essay instead of five reading questions, and the writing is a story or personal piece instead of an article, speech or letter. Some schools use coursework, 4EA1 slash 03, instead of this paper. Each branch is one question type: read the question, find the key words, plan, write, check. Then five spoken questions. Draft for teacher review. (Source: spec pages 6, 13 and 29.)

children.note: Section A has one essay question, Question 1, worth 30 marks. It is on one poem or prose text from Part 2 of the Anthology, and the text is printed for you in the exam. 12 marks are for understanding the text, assessment objective 1. 18 marks are for how the writer uses language and structure, assessment objective 2. Pearson advises 45 minutes. (Source: spec page 13.)

The question asks how the writer does something, for example how the writer creates feelings of isolation, or tries to interest the reader. Three bullet points follow. The third bullet point always asks about language and structure. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 3.)

Underline the focus word, such as isolation, sympathy or interest. Every paragraph must link back to it. Answer this question; do not write everything you know about the text. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 68.)

Use the time to remind yourself of the text, not to read it from scratch. Choose points from the beginning, middle and end. Put a language or structure point in every part of the plan. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: plan for about 5 minutes. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 68.)

Make a point about the focus, give a short quotation, then explain its effect on the reader. Name a device only if you can say what it does. Use different quotations for your ideas points and your language points. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: write for about 35 minutes and check for 5. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 7.)
Save five minutes. Read your answer again and check it for each of these, and check your spelling and punctuation. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Language and structure added on at the end, though they are worth 18 marks. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 5.
Naming devices without explaining their effect. This is called feature-spotting. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 7.
Writing everything you know about the poem instead of answering this question. June 2023 Paper 2 report page 5.
Guessing at things the text does not support, for example saying the boy hurt himself on purpose. June 2023 Paper 2 report page 6.
Long quotations, or the same quotation used for two different marks. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 5.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many marks is Section A? Answer: Thirty: 12 for understanding the text and 18 for language and structure. (Source: SAMs PDF page 52; spec page 13.)
Ask: Do you need to bring the Anthology? Answer: No. The text is given to you in the exam. (Source: SAMs PDF page 52; spec page 13.)
Ask: What does the third bullet point always ask about? Answer: Language and structure. (Source: SAMs PDF page 52; spec page 13.)
Ask: Can one quotation earn two different marks? Answer: Not for the same point. Use different quotations for different points. (Source: SAMs PDF page 52; spec page 13.)
Ask: How long does Pearson advise for Section A? Answer: 45 minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 52; spec page 13.)

Section B gives you three writing tasks and you choose one. Question 2 always begins: Write about a time when you, or someone you know. In June 2025 it was someone who had a visitor. It is worth 30 marks: 18 for communication, assessment objective 4, and 12 for accuracy, assessment objective 5. Your answer can be real or imagined. Pearson advises 45 minutes for Section B. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)
Listen for who the writing is about, you or someone you know, and what happened to them. Choose the task you have most ideas for. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)

Mark the key event, such as a visitor or an unexpected experience. Your whole piece must be about that event. A story learned before the exam, with one line added at the end, rarely works. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)

Plan a beginning, middle and end, and know your ending before you start. Do not spend long on the lead-up. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: plan for about 5 minutes. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 68.)

Open with a hook. Choose a few moments and describe them with detail and feeling, not every step of the day. Vary how your sentences start and how long they are. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: write for about 35 minutes, then check for 5. (Source: June 2023 Paper 2 report page 31.)
Save five minutes. Read your answer again and check it for each of these, and check your spelling and punctuation. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
A dry, factual account where one thing just happens after another. June 2023 Paper 2 report page 31.
Telling every detail, such as each step of a trip. June 2023 Paper 2 report page 31.
Spending too long on the lead-up, so the key moment comes late. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 34.
A plot that stays flat, with no rise in tension. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 34.
A story prepared earlier, with a link to the task added at the end. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How does Question 2 always begin? Answer: Write about a time when you, or someone you know. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)
Ask: Must your story be true? Answer: No. It can be real or imagined. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)
Ask: How many marks is it? Answer: Thirty: 18 for communicating and 12 for accuracy. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)
Ask: Should you tell every detail of the day? Answer: No. Choose a few moments and develop them. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)
Ask: What should you know before you start writing? Answer: How your piece will end. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)

Question 3 always asks you to write a story with a given title. In June 2025 the title was The Celebration. In the sample paper it was Left Behind. It is worth 30 marks: 18 for communication, assessment objective 4, and 12 for accuracy, assessment objective 5. Your answer can be real or imagined. Pearson advises 45 minutes for Section B. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)
Listen for the title. Say it out loud and ask what it could mean. It can be literal or symbolic: something left behind can be a real object, or a feeling. (Source: SAMs mark scheme PDF page 81.)
Mark each word of the title. The title is the purpose of your story, so the whole story must fit it. A very dark story may not fit a happy title. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)
Plan the whole shape, including the ending, so the story does not run out of steam. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: plan for about 5 minutes. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)

Hook the reader at the start. Keep the title idea running through the whole story, not just at the end. If characters speak, punctuate the speech carefully. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: write for about 35 minutes, then check for 5. (Source: June 2023 Paper 2 report page 39.)
Save five minutes. Read your answer again and check it for each of these, and check your spelling and punctuation. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
A dark version that does not really fit the title. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.
A strong start that loses momentum towards the end. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.
One line added at the end, such as this was a celebration. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.
The title idea dropped in at the end, not woven through. June 2023 Paper 2 report page 39.
Common, everyday adjectives instead of fresh description. June 2023 Paper 2 report page 39.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What does Question 3 always give you? Answer: A title for your story. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)
Ask: Can the title be symbolic? Answer: Yes. It can be literal or symbolic. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)
Ask: Where should the title idea appear? Answer: All through the story, not just at the end. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)
Ask: Why did some strong openings lose marks in 2025? Answer: The stories lost momentum towards the end, because of weak planning. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)
Ask: How long does Pearson advise for Section B? Answer: 45 minutes. (Source: SAMs PDF page 62.)

Question 4 gives you two pictures and a line of words. You write a story that begins, or ends, with that line. In June 2025 it began: It was quiet in town that evening. You may use one picture to help, but you do not have to. It is worth 30 marks: 18 for communication, assessment objective 4, and 12 for accuracy, assessment objective 5. Your answer can be real or imagined. Pearson advises 45 minutes for Section B. (Source: SAMs PDF page 63.)
Listen for the given line, and whether your story must begin or end with it. Then look at both pictures. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.)
Mark the exact words of the line. Use them exactly, as your first words or your last words. The pictures are only there to help. (Source: SAMs mark scheme PDF page 82.)
If you plan a twist, plant small clues for it early so the ending makes sense. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: plan for about 5 minutes. (Source: June 2023 Paper 2 report page 48.)

Build the setting with the senses: buildings, streets and weather. Control the tension with the rhythm of your sentences and paragraphs. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: write for about 35 minutes, then check for 5. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 56.)
Save five minutes. Read your answer again and check it for each of these, and check your spelling and punctuation. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Predictable stories, with few surprising but believable twists. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 56.
A twist ending with no clues earlier in the story. June 2023 Paper 2 report page 48.
Lots of action, but little description or real suspense. June 2023 Paper 2 report page 48.
Too long on reasons and preparations before the story starts. June 2023 Paper 2 report page 48.
Cliches, especially about danger. June 2023 Paper 2 report page 48.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many pictures are there? Answer: Two. (Source: SAMs PDF pages 62 and 63.)
Ask: Must you write about a picture? Answer: No. You may use one to help, but you do not have to. (Source: SAMs PDF pages 62 and 63.)
Ask: The given line may begin the story. Where else can it go? Answer: At the end of the story. (Source: SAMs PDF pages 62 and 63.)
Ask: What makes a twist ending work? Answer: Small clues planted earlier, so it makes sense. (Source: SAMs PDF pages 62 and 63.)
Ask: How many marks is it? Answer: Thirty: 18 for communicating and 12 for accuracy. (Source: SAMs PDF pages 62 and 63.)
