nodeData.note: Edexcel International GCSE Chemistry, Paper 1, code 4 C H 1 slash 1 C. Two hours, 110 marks, sixty-one point one percent of the qualification. A calculator may be used. It tests the core content: everything not in bold and without a C reference. Questions may come from all four topics. Question styles are multiple choice, short answers, calculations and longer answers. Each branch is one question type: read the question, find the key words, plan, write, check. Then five spoken questions. Draft: needs review by a subject teacher. (Source: spec pages 7 and 27.)

children.note: State, give and name all mean the same thing: recall a fact. These parts are usually worth one or two marks and test knowledge, assessment objective 1. Spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 45.)
Listen for how many things you must give. The number of marks tells you how many facts are needed. (Source: June 2025 report page 8.)
Underline the command word and the exact thing asked for, such as two observations or a definition. (Source: June 2025 report page 8.)
Recall the fact in your head first. For a definition, use the exact words from the specification. (Source: June 2025 report page 37.)
Give only the number of answers asked for. Spell key words in full and write clearly. (Source: June 2025 report page 33.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Listing extra answers when one is wrong. This cancels the mark. June 2025 report pages 8 and 33.
Words that are hard to read or not fully formed, such as boron. June 2025 report pages 6 and 7.
Swapping a key word in a definition, such as chemical formula for molecular formula. June 2025 report page 37.
Repeating the same idea twice, such as air and oxygen for rusting. June 2025 report page 43.
Giving an answer that is already in the question, such as carbon monoxide. June 2025 report page 33.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What do state, give and name ask you to do? Answer: Recall a fact. They all mean the same thing. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: A question asks for two observations. How many do you give? Answer: Exactly two. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: What happens if you list three answers and one is wrong? Answer: You can lose the mark. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: What two things does iron need to rust? Answer: Water and oxygen. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: What should you do with a definition from the specification? Answer: Learn it word for word and use those exact words. (Source: spec page 45.)

Describe means give an account in linked statements. You do not need to give reasons. In Paper 1 this is often what you would see, or how to do a chemical test. These parts are usually worth two or three marks and mostly test knowledge, assessment objective 1. Spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 45.)
Listen for what you must describe: what you would see, how to do a test, or what happens to the particles. (Source: June 2025 report page 8.)
Mark the word describe and the substance named. If it says observations, give only things you can see, hear or feel. (Source: June 2025 report page 9.)
Count the marks and jot one point for each mark. For a test, write the reagent first and then the result. (Source: June 2025 report page 44.)
Write each point as a short sentence. Name the full reagent and use exact words, like precipitate, with the colour. (Source: June 2025 report page 45.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Giving a product as an observation. You cannot see lithium hydroxide form. June 2025 report page 9.
Describing a different metal, such as a flame for lithium. June 2025 report page 8.
An incomplete reagent, or leaving out the word precipitate, in a test. June 2025 report pages 44 and 45.
Leaving out the pH value, or not saying the solution is alkaline. June 2025 report page 10.
Saying gases are harmful when the answer needs toxic. June 2025 report page 76.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What does describe mean? Answer: Give an account in linked statements. You do not need a reason. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Is lithium hydroxide forms an observation? Answer: No. You cannot see it form. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Give one thing you see when lithium is added to water. Answer: For example, it gets smaller and disappears. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: What two parts does a chemical test answer need? Answer: The reagent you add, and what you see. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Universal indicator is added to a strong alkali. What happens? Answer: It turns blue, and the pH is between ten and fourteen. (Source: spec page 45.)

Explain means give a reason. Every point must say why. In Paper 1 this is often about structure and bonding, melting points, or redox. These parts are usually worth two or three marks and test knowledge and applying it, assessment objectives 1 and 2. Spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 45.)
Listen for the word explain. A fact alone is not enough; you need the reason too. Each mark is one linked step. (Source: June 2025 report page 29.)
Mark every term in the question. If two terms are asked about, such as saturated and hydrocarbon, explain both. (Source: June 2025 report page 28.)
Decide the type of structure first: simple molecules, giant covalent, ionic or metal. Then choose the right bond or force. (Source: June 2025 report pages 40 and 64.)
Link ideas with because and so. For example: the forces between molecules are stronger, so more energy is needed to overcome them. (Source: June 2025 report page 41.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Using intermolecular forces for diamond or graphite, which have no molecules. June 2025 report pages 64 and 66.
Saying covalent bonds break when a simple molecule like hexane melts. June 2025 report page 40.
Explaining only one of the terms in the question. June 2025 report pages 28 and 29.
Giving the redox definition without linking it to the equation given. June 2025 report pages 46 and 47.
Vague words like more energy, or nucleus instead of nuclei. June 2025 report pages 64 and 73.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What must every explain answer contain? Answer: A reason. Link the fact to why it happens. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Why does hexane melt at a higher temperature than butane? Answer: Hexane has stronger forces between its molecules, so more energy is needed to overcome them. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Why does diamond have a very high melting point? Answer: It is giant covalent. Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, which needs a lot of energy. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: What is a covalent bond? Answer: The attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the two atoms. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: What does saturated mean for a hydrocarbon? Answer: It has only single bonds between its carbon atoms. (Source: spec page 45.)

Calculate means get a number and show your working. In Paper 1 you may work out an R f value, relative formula mass, moles, reacting masses, percentage yield, empirical formula, or energy change. These parts are usually worth two to five marks and mostly test applying knowledge, assessment objective 2. A calculator is allowed. The specification does not mention a formula sheet, so learn the equations. Spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec pages 7, 13, 21 and 45.)
Listen for what you must find, the units, and how to round it, such as to two significant figures. (Source: June 2025 report page 21.)
Underline every number and its unit. Note which mass belongs to which substance. If a sign is needed, write a reminder. (Source: June 2025 report pages 88 and 90.)
Choose the equation and say it in words: moles equals mass divided by relative formula mass. Check the ratio in the balanced equation. (Source: June 2025 report pages 48 and 49.)
Show every step, with units, and put the final answer on the answer line. Working can still earn marks if an earlier step is wrong. (Source: June 2025 report pages 3 and 49.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Not rounding as asked, or measuring the solvent front from the wrong place. June 2025 report pages 21 to 23.
Using atomic numbers instead of relative atomic masses. June 2025 report pages 24 and 78.
Using the mole ratio the wrong way round, multiplying instead of dividing. June 2025 report page 48.
Leaving out the minus sign, or not dividing by one thousand. June 2025 report page 88.
Using the wrong mass, or an earlier answer instead of the value given. June 2025 report pages 50 and 88.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How do you work out moles from a mass? Answer: Moles equals mass divided by relative formula mass. (Source: spec pages 7, 13, 21 and 45.)
Ask: How do you work out percentage yield? Answer: Actual yield divided by theoretical yield, times one hundred. (Source: spec pages 7, 13, 21 and 45.)
Ask: What is the heat energy equation? Answer: Q equals m c delta T: mass of water, times specific heat capacity, times temperature change. (Source: spec pages 7, 13, 21 and 45.)
Ask: How do you find an R f value? Answer: Distance moved by the spot divided by distance moved by the solvent, both measured from the baseline. (Source: spec pages 7, 13, 21 and 45.)
Ask: Why should you always show your working? Answer: You can still get marks for later steps if one step is wrong. (Source: spec pages 7, 13, 21 and 45.)

Plot means mark points accurately on a grid and draw a line of best fit. Then you may read values from the graph or spot an odd result. This tests experimental skills and data, assessment objective 3. In June 2025 the graph parts gave about six fairly easy marks. Spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec pages 28 and 46; June 2025 report page 57.)
Listen for what to plot and for any instruction, such as draw two straight lines. (Source: June 2025 report page 57.)
Mark plot, line of best fit and anomalous. Check the label and unit on each axis. (Source: spec page 46.)
Get a sharp pencil and a ruler. If the axes are not given, choose a suitable scale and label both axes with units. (Source: spec page 46.)
Plot each point with a small neat cross. Circle any point that does not fit. Draw a thin line of best fit that follows the trend. (Source: June 2025 report pages 57 and 60.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Thick lines of best fit drawn with a blunt pencil. June 2025 report page 57.
Drawing a curve when the question said two straight lines. June 2025 report page 57.
Putting correct readings in the wrong answer spaces. June 2025 report page 57.
Copying values from the table instead of reading them from the graph. June 2025 report page 57.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What does plot mean? Answer: Mark points accurately on a grid, then draw a line of best fit. (Source: spec pages 28 and 46; June 2025 report page 57.)
Ask: What is an anomalous result? Answer: A result that does not fit the pattern of the others. (Source: spec pages 28 and 46; June 2025 report page 57.)
Ask: Should your line go through the anomalous point? Answer: No. Follow the trend of the other points. (Source: spec pages 28 and 46; June 2025 report page 57.)
Ask: What does each axis need? Answer: A label with units, and a suitable scale. (Source: spec pages 28 and 46; June 2025 report page 57.)
Ask: Two lines of best fit cross. Where do you read the answer? Answer: From the graph, at the point where the two lines meet. (Source: spec pages 28 and 46; June 2025 report page 57.)

Practical questions ask you to plan, improve or judge an experiment. You may name variables to control, suggest an improvement, or explain an odd result. This tests experimental skills, assessment objective 3. The examiners said these were the weakest parts of the June 2025 paper. They are usually worth two to four marks. Spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 report page 3.)
Listen for the aim of the experiment and the task: improve it, explain an odd result, or name a control variable. (Source: June 2025 report page 84.)
Mark the word accuracy or reliability. They are different. Repeating and taking a mean improves reliability, not accuracy. (Source: June 2025 report page 55.)
Find the biggest problem in the method, such as heat lost to the air. Ask which way it would push the result. (Source: June 2025 report page 63.)
Give one change and say why it helps. For example, use a polystyrene cup instead of a glass beaker, to reduce heat loss. (Source: June 2025 report pages 55 and 56.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Suggesting repeats and a mean when the question asks about accuracy. June 2025 report page 55.
Saying a change prevents heat loss, instead of reduces it. June 2025 report page 56.
Blaming a small slip, like misreading a thermometer, for a big odd result. June 2025 report pages 57 and 63.
Adding a second, wrong reason after a good one. June 2025 report page 60.
Explaining a control variable by time, not by its effect on the result. June 2025 report page 84.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Does repeating and taking a mean improve accuracy? Answer: No. It improves reliability. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 report page 3.)
Ask: Name one way to reduce heat loss in a temperature experiment. Answer: Use a polystyrene cup instead of a glass beaker. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 report page 3.)
Ask: What is a control variable? Answer: Something you keep the same so the test is fair. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 report page 3.)
Ask: Why keep the volume of water the same when burning fuels? Answer: So the same amount of energy gives a temperature change you can compare fairly. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 report page 3.)
Ask: What should you ask about any error you suggest? Answer: Would it change the result in the right direction, and by enough? (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 report page 3.)

These questions ask you to write a formula or a balanced equation, add state symbols, or draw a molecule, such as a dot and cross diagram or a repeating unit. They are usually worth one or two marks each and test assessment objectives 1 and 2. The examiners asked students to practise completing, balancing, and adding state symbols. Spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 13; June 2025 report page 91.)
Listen for what is wanted: a word equation, a balanced equation, state symbols, or a drawing of a molecule. (Source: spec page 13.)
Mark balanced, state symbols, and every substance named. Write the correct formula of each one first. (Source: June 2025 report page 52.)
Work out the big numbers below the answer line. Count each type of atom on both sides. Never change the small numbers in a formula. (Source: June 2025 report page 27.)
Write the final equation neatly on the line. Oxygen is O two, not O. Check that every carbon atom has four bonds. (Source: June 2025 report pages 31 and 75.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Writing O for oxygen instead of O two, or a small o in carbon dioxide. June 2025 report page 31.
A wrong formula, such as only one sodium in sodium sulfate. June 2025 report page 52.
Missing or wrong state symbols. June 2025 report pages 52 to 54.
Messy crossings out over the final answer. June 2025 report pages 26 and 27.
No lone pairs on chlorine, or a double bond left in a repeating unit. June 2025 report pages 70 and 74.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What is the formula of oxygen gas? Answer: O two. Oxygen atoms go in pairs. (Source: spec page 13; June 2025 report page 91.)
Ask: What are the four state symbols? Answer: s for solid, l for liquid, g for gas, and a q for aqueous. (Source: spec page 13; June 2025 report page 91.)
Ask: When balancing, what can you change? Answer: Only the big numbers in front. Never the small numbers inside a formula. (Source: spec page 13; June 2025 report page 91.)
Ask: How many bonds does each carbon atom make? Answer: Four. (Source: spec page 13; June 2025 report page 91.)
Ask: What happens to the double bond in a repeating unit? Answer: It becomes a single bond. (Source: spec page 13; June 2025 report page 91.)

children.topic: Extended answer: five or six marks
children.note: Extended open-response questions are worth five or six marks. In June 2025 there was a six-mark question on the structure of graphite, and a five-mark question on how ethane and ethene react with bromine. They test knowledge and applying it, assessment objectives 1 and 2. Spend about six to eight minutes. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 7; June 2025 report pages 66 and 81.)
Listen for every part. If two substances are named, you must write about both. (Source: June 2025 report page 81.)
Mark the topic, the command word, and any guide in the question, such as refer to structure and bonding. (Source: June 2025 report page 66.)
Jot one bullet point for each mark, plus one spare. Cover the bonding, the structure and the property, and link them. (Source: June 2025 report pages 68 and 91.)
Bullet points are fine. Give each point once, in exact words. Link every property back to the structure. (Source: June 2025 report page 68.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Not mentioning bonding when the question asks about it. June 2025 report page 66.
Saying three covalent bonds, instead of bonded to three other carbon atoms. June 2025 report page 66.
Good ideas, like layers sliding, not linked to the structure. June 2025 report pages 66 and 69.
Writing about only one of the two substances, or only what you see. June 2025 report page 81.
Handwriting where ene and ane look the same. June 2025 report pages 3 and 81.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many marks are extended answers usually worth? Answer: Five or six marks. (Source: spec page 7; June 2025 report pages 66 and 81.)
Ask: Can you use bullet points? Answer: Yes. The examiners encourage them if they are clear and do not repeat. (Source: spec page 7; June 2025 report pages 66 and 81.)
Ask: Why is graphite soft? Answer: The forces between its layers are weak, so the layers can slide over each other. (Source: spec page 7; June 2025 report pages 66 and 81.)
Ask: Why does graphite conduct electricity? Answer: It has delocalised electrons that can move through the structure. (Source: spec page 7; June 2025 report pages 66 and 81.)
Ask: What do you see when ethene is added to bromine water? Answer: The orange colour disappears. It turns colourless. (Source: spec page 7; June 2025 report pages 66 and 81.)

nodeData.note: Edexcel International GCSE Chemistry, Paper 2, code 4 C H 1 slash 2 C. One hour and fifteen minutes, 70 marks, thirty-eight point nine percent of the qualification. A calculator may be used. Paper 2 tests all the content, including the extra content in bold with a C reference, such as concentration and gas volume calculations, energy level diagrams, equilibrium, titrations, salt preparation, electrolysis half-equations, and esters. This is how it differs from Paper 1, which is two hours, 110 marks, and core content only. Question styles are multiple choice, short answers, calculations and longer answers. Each branch is one question type: read the question, find the key words, plan, write, check. Then five spoken questions. Draft: needs review by a subject teacher. (Source: spec pages 7, 8 and 27.)

children.note: State, give and name mean recall a fact. In Paper 2 these are often one-mark parts, such as a chemical test, a fuel, or a key word like reversible. They test knowledge, assessment objective 1. Paper 2 is seventy five minutes for seventy marks, so spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 45.)
Listen for exactly what is asked. In June 2025 one question asked about subatomic particles, not atomic number. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 18.)
Underline the exact thing asked for, such as a use, a test, or a word to describe the reaction. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 5.)
Recall the exact word from the specification. Reversible and reverse are not the same word. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 64.)
Write the whole answer. For a gas test, say what you do and what you see. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 63.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in June 2025 Paper 2.
Writing aircraft without the word fuel. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 5.
Saying energy is released instead of heat is released. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 6.
Same atomic number and different mass number, instead of protons and neutrons. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 18.
A glowing splint, or a squeaky pop with no lit splint, for hydrogen. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 63.
Saying a reverse reaction instead of a reversible reaction. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 64.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What is the test for hydrogen? Answer: Hold a lit splint at the mouth of the tube. It burns with a squeaky pop. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: What does exothermic mean? Answer: Heat is given out to the surroundings. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: What are isotopes? Answer: Atoms with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Name a use of the kerosene fraction. Answer: Aircraft fuel, or jet fuel. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: What do we call a reaction that can go both ways? Answer: A reversible reaction. (Source: spec page 45.)

Describe means give an account, with no reason needed. In Paper 2 this is often what you would see in a reaction, a colour change, or a smell. These parts are usually worth one or two marks and test knowledge, assessment objective 1. Paper 2 is seventy five minutes for seventy marks, so spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 45.)
Listen for the word observation. You must give things you can see, hear, feel or smell. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 43.)
Mark the substances named, and whether you need a start colour and an end colour. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 40.)
For a colour change, say both colours in the right order: from orange to green. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 40.)
Use exact words, such as fizzing, sweet smell, or colour change. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in June 2025 Paper 2.
Saying a gas is produced. That is not an observation. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 43.
Orange and green the wrong way round for acidified dichromate. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 40.
Just a smell, or a strong smell, for an ester. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.
Saying colour, not colour change, for an indicator. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 50.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Is a gas is produced an observation? Answer: No. Say fizzing, or bubbles, instead. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Ethanol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate. What colour change do you see? Answer: Orange to green. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: What does an ester smell like? Answer: Sweet or fruity. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Sodium carbonate is added to ethanoic acid. Give two things you see. Answer: Fizzing, and the solid gets smaller and disappears. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Why use an indicator in a titration? Answer: To see a clear colour change at the end point. (Source: spec page 45.)

Explain means give a reason for each point. In Paper 2 this is often about rates and collisions, equilibrium, or why substances conduct electricity. These parts are usually worth two to four marks and test knowledge and applying it, assessment objectives 1 and 2. Paper 2 is seventy five minutes for seventy marks, so spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 45.)
Listen for the change being made, such as raising the temperature or the pressure. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 65.)
Mark every substance named. If there are two, explain both, such as water and magnesium chloride. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 30.)
Say what happens first, then the reason. For example: the yield increases, because the forward reaction is endothermic. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 66.)
Use the key words: more frequent collisions, successful collisions, covalent, ionic, moles of gas. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 12.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in June 2025 Paper 2.
No mention of more successful collisions when temperature rises. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 13.
Saying delocalised electrons, or intermolecular forces, for magnesium chloride. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 28.
Not saying water is covalent and magnesium chloride is ionic. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 30.
Saying the yield increases, but not that the forward reaction is endothermic. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 66.
Saying the yield changes when the moles of gas are equal on both sides. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 69.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate? Answer: Particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent, and more collisions have the activation energy. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: The forward reaction is endothermic. What happens to the yield if you heat it? Answer: The yield increases. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Both sides have the same moles of gas. What does more pressure do to the yield? Answer: Nothing. The yield does not change. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: Why does pure water not conduct electricity? Answer: It is covalent, so there are no ions free to move. (Source: spec page 45.)
Ask: When does magnesium chloride conduct? Answer: When molten or dissolved, because the ions are free to move. (Source: spec page 45.)

Calculate means get a number and show your working. Paper 2 adds two calculations that are not in Paper 1: concentration in a titration, and volumes of gas. You may also work out a relative atomic mass. These parts are usually worth three or four marks and test applying knowledge, assessment objective 2. A calculator is allowed. There is no formula sheet in the specification, so learn the equations. Paper 2 is seventy five minutes for seventy marks, so spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 13, statements 1.34C and 1.35C.)
Listen for how to give the answer: one decimal place, two decimal places, or standard form. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 20.)
Underline every number and unit. If a volume is in centimetres cubed, divide by one thousand to get decimetres cubed. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 71.)
Find the mole ratio in the balanced equation before you start. It may mean dividing by two, or multiplying by two. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 59.)
Show every step in order. You can get marks for later steps even if one step is wrong. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 57.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in June 2025 Paper 2.
Not giving the answer to one decimal place, as asked. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 20.
Not dividing by two, using the mole ratio in the equation. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 57.
Not dividing by one thousand, and not using the eighty percent. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 71.
Not multiplying by two for the two moles of product. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 72.
Not giving the final answer in standard form. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 73.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How do you work out moles from a solution? Answer: Concentration times volume in decimetres cubed. (Source: spec page 13, statements 1.34C and 1.35C.)
Ask: How do you change centimetres cubed into decimetres cubed? Answer: Divide by one thousand. (Source: spec page 13, statements 1.34C and 1.35C.)

Ask: What volume does one mole of any gas take up at room temperature and pressure? Answer: Twenty four decimetres cubed, which is twenty four thousand centimetres cubed. (Source: spec page 13, statements 1.34C and 1.35C.)

Ask: The equation shows one mole of acid reacts with two moles of alkali. What do you do with the moles of alkali? Answer: Divide by two to get the moles of acid. (Source: spec page 13, statements 1.34C and 1.35C.)
Ask: Why should you always show your working? Answer: You can still get marks for later steps if one step is wrong. (Source: spec page 13, statements 1.34C and 1.35C.)

Paper 2 may ask you to sketch a curve, such as gas made over time, or draw an energy level diagram with labelled arrows. Energy level diagrams and reaction profiles are Paper 2 content, in bold in the specification. The examiners asked students to use a ruler and draw arrows accurately. These parts are worth two to five marks. Paper 2 is seventy five minutes for seventy marks, so spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec pages 21 and 22, statements 3.5C and 3.14C.)
Listen for the type of reaction. If it says exothermic, the products must be lower than the reactants. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 17.)
Mark what must be labelled, such as delta H and activation energy. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 17.)
Get a sharp pencil and a ruler. Decide where the curve starts and where it ends. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 74.)
Draw single-headed arrows the right length and in the right direction, and label each one. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 16.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in June 2025 Paper 2.
Not finishing the curve with a horizontal line. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 8.
A curve that does not start at the origin. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 9.
A straight line instead of a curve. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 10.
Double-headed arrows, or arrows too short. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 16.
An arrow with no label, so it could be delta H or activation energy. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 17.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Where must a curve of gas volume against time start? Answer: At the origin, where both values are zero. (Source: spec pages 21 and 22, statements 3.5C and 3.14C.)
Ask: Why does the curve end with a horizontal line? Answer: The reaction has stopped because a reactant is used up. (Source: spec pages 21 and 22, statements 3.5C and 3.14C.)
Ask: In an exothermic energy level diagram, where are the products? Answer: Lower than the reactants. (Source: spec pages 21 and 22, statements 3.5C and 3.14C.)
Ask: Which way does the delta H arrow point for an exothermic reaction? Answer: Downwards, from the reactants to the products. (Source: spec pages 21 and 22, statements 3.5C and 3.14C.)
Ask: Where does the activation energy arrow go? Answer: Upwards, from the reactants to the top of the hump. (Source: spec pages 21 and 22, statements 3.5C and 3.14C.)

Paper 2 practical questions in June 2025 covered a titration, making pure dry crystals of a salt, and making an ester. Titrations and salt preparation are Paper 2 content. In the June 2025 report summary, the examiners said practical work was twenty two percent of the paper, and told students to revise it all. These parts are usually worth one to four marks and test experimental skills, assessment objective 3. Paper 2 is seventy five minutes for seventy marks, so spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec pages 18, 19 and 26.)
Listen for the method being asked about, and how many decimal places to use. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 54.)
Mark the word concordant. Concordant results are within zero point two zero centimetres cubed of each other. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 55.)
For a method, jot bullet points in order first: heat, cool, filter, dry. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 60.)
Write burette readings to two decimal places, ending in zero or five. Give each step of a method in order. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 51.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in June 2025 Paper 2.
Writing 28.1 instead of 28.10 for a burette reading. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 51.
Misreading the meniscus, at 32.20 instead of 32.25. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 53.
Using the wrong results for the mean titre. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 55.
Leaving out cooling and filtering when making crystals. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 62.
Mentioning a water bath, but not that ethanol is flammable. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 45.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What are concordant results? Answer: Results within zero point two zero centimetres cubed of each other. (Source: spec pages 18, 19 and 26.)
Ask: How many decimal places for a burette reading? Answer: Two, ending in zero or five. (Source: spec pages 18, 19 and 26.)

Ask: Give the four steps to get dry crystals from a salt solution. Answer: Heat to evaporate some water, leave to cool, filter, then dry the crystals in a warm oven. (Source: spec pages 18, 19 and 26.)
Ask: Why heat ethanol with a water bath, not a flame? Answer: Ethanol is flammable. (Source: spec pages 18, 19 and 26.)
Ask: Why is a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid added when making an ester? Answer: It is a catalyst. It speeds up the reaction. (Source: spec pages 18, 19 and 26.)

These questions ask you to write a formula, balance an equation, write an ionic half-equation, draw a dot and cross diagram, or draw a displayed formula. Half-equations at electrodes and the formula of an ester are Paper 2 content. They are usually worth one or two marks each and test assessment objectives 1 and 2. Paper 2 is seventy five minutes for seventy marks, so spend about one minute per mark. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec pages 13, 15 and 26.)
Listen for what is wanted: a formula, a balanced equation, a half-equation, or a diagram. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 23.)
Mark the word ionic or covalent. If it says ionic, draw ions with charges, not shared pairs. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 23.)
Write the correct formula of each substance first. Then count each type of atom, and each charge, on both sides. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 36.)
Write the final answer neatly. Remember halogens go in pairs, so chlorine is Cl two. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 37.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in June 2025 Paper 2.
Writing MgCl instead of MgCl two for magnesium chloride. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 7.
Wrong charges on the ions, such as not two plus and two minus. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 26.
Writing Cl instead of Cl two in a half-equation. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 37.
Putting twos or threes in front of carbon dioxide and water when they are not needed. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 41.
A wrong displayed formula for ethyl ethanoate, with an extra oxygen. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 48.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What is the formula of magnesium chloride? Answer: Mg Cl two. (Source: spec pages 13, 15 and 26.)
Ask: What are the charges on a magnesium ion and an oxide ion? Answer: Magnesium is two plus. Oxide is two minus. (Source: spec pages 13, 15 and 26.)
Ask: Write the half-equation for chloride ions at the anode, in words. Answer: Two Cl minus gives Cl two plus two electrons. (Source: spec pages 13, 15 and 26.)
Ask: Chloride ions lose electrons. Is this oxidation or reduction? Answer: Oxidation. Loss of electrons is oxidation. (Source: spec pages 13, 15 and 26.)
Ask: How many bonds does carbon make, and how many does oxygen make? Answer: Carbon makes four. Oxygen makes two. Hydrogen makes one. (Source: spec pages 13, 15 and 26.)

children.topic: Extended answer: four or five marks
children.note: Paper 2 longer answers are worth four or five marks. In June 2025 they included why water and magnesium chloride conduct or not, how temperature changes the rate, and how to make dry crystals. The specification does not give a fixed number of marks, so this comes from the June 2025 report. They test knowledge and applying it, assessment objectives 1 and 2, and sometimes 3. Spend about five or six minutes. That time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 8; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 28.)
Listen for every substance and every condition named. You must write about each one. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 28.)
Mark the topic word, such as conduct, rate or crystals. Each mark is one key idea. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)
Jot one bullet point for each mark. The examiners say this is a good idea. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 74.)
Give the type of bonding first, then the reason. Do not add extra ideas, like delocalised electrons, that are not true here. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in June 2025 Paper 2.
Saying water is ionic. If it were ionic it would conduct. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 31.
Saying electrons carry the charge in an ionic compound. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 30.
No mention of more frequent or more successful collisions. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.
Leaving out filtering when making dry crystals. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 61.
Adding delocalised electrons when they are not there. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 74.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Can you use bullet points in a longer answer? Answer: Yes. The examiners say jotting bullet points first is a good idea. (Source: spec page 8; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 28.)
Ask: What carries the charge in molten magnesium chloride? Answer: Ions that are free to move. Not electrons. (Source: spec page 8; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 28.)
Ask: Why does solid magnesium chloride not conduct? Answer: Its ions are held in a lattice and cannot move. (Source: spec page 8; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 28.)

Ask: Give the four points for why heat speeds up a reaction. Answer: Rate increases, particles move faster, more frequent collisions, and more successful collisions. (Source: spec page 8; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 28.)
Ask: Does magnesium chloride have intermolecular forces? Answer: No. It is ionic, with strong attraction between ions. (Source: spec page 8; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 28.)
